To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dopamine neuron–specific leptin signaling reduces some aspects of hedonic feeding but does not amelio- rate the obesity phenotype of leptin-deficient mice.
dopamine neuron-restricted leptin receptor signaling reduces some aspects of feeding and activity but does exacerbate the obesity of leptin receptor deficient male mice.
Lepr signaling in dopamine neurons regulates some aspects of food intake but does not amelio-rate the obesity phenotype in leptin receptor–deficient mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of dopamine neurons in energy homeostasis.
the role of dopamine in the control of food intake and energy balance.
the role of leptin signaling in the control food intake and body weight, and we use mice as our experimental model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the LeprDAT mouse model provides evidence that direct leptin signaling to dopamine neurons reduces food reward and activity and that these effects do not fully compensate for the obesity phenotype of mice lacking Lepr.

the LeprDAT male mouse model demonstrates that dopamine neuron–restricted Lepr signaling reduces some aspects of feeding and activity but does little to prevent the obesity of Lepr-deficiency in male mice.
Lepr signaling in dopamine neurons has little impact on body weight and energy homeostatic regulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dopamine neuron–restricted Lepr signaling reduces some aspects of feeding behavior and activity but does exacerbate the obesity of Lepr-deficiency in male mice.
dopamine neuron–restricted Lepr signaling is sufficient to mediate some aspects of leptin action but is insufficient to fully mediate all of leptin’s effects on food intake or body weight.
the obesity of LeprNULL mice cannot be ameliorated by selective dopamine neuron–restricted Lepr signaling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
leptin signaling in dopamine neurons is not sufficient to prevent or ameliorate the obese phenotype of LeprNULL mice.

leptin receptor signaling in dopamine neurons does not appear to be a critical component of energy homeostasis and that the obesity of LeprNULL mice is not due to a failure to activate the reward value of palatable food.
leptin-induced suppression and hedonic responses to food are not dependent on direct Lepr signaling within dopamine neurons.
